newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q3 GDP revised downwards but above forecasts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q3 GDP revised downwards but above forecasts.

text.p: The U.S. economy in the third quarter grew at a slower pace than an earlier reading had shown, but the gross domestic product (GDP) data was stronger than Wall Street economists had predicted.
The Commerce Department reported on Wednesday a revised 2.0 percent rise in GDP versus a prior reading of 2.2 percent.
In a Reuter poll, U.S. economists had predicted a revised 1.7 percent growth rate for GDP in the third quarter.
"I don't think it changes the picture for the current quarter," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"The inventory overhang is still there but not as much as estimated," Carson said. "The number came in according to script - a little less inventories and more final demand."
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.

"This is slightly higher (than Wall Street estimates) but it really doesn't change the assessment of what's happening in the economy," said Larry Chimerine, chief economist at Economic Strategy Institute.
Commerce reported a drop in inventories to a 32.8 percent rate from its previously reported number of 39.6 percent.
"The numbers were no real surprise," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.

"Perhaps there was initial disappointment earlier on (in the marketplace) that growth wasn't slower than even 2.0 percent. The undercurrent bullishness in the market is still there and probably will be retained until at least the end of next week when we get the employment report," Flanagan noted.

Commerce said consumer spending grew at a revised annual rate of $6.7 billion a year or 0.6 percent in the third quarter compared with the second quarter's $38.5 billion or 3.4 percent. A month ago it said spending grew even more weakly at a $5.2 billion rate or 0.4 percent.
The revised 0.6 percent increase in consumer spending for the third quarter remained the weakest since a 1.0 percent drop in the fourth quarter of 1991, Commerce said.

"I think there may have been a bit of surprise...that you didn't get a little more of an increase in final sales and a little more strength in consumption, but the overall result was about as expected," said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc.
Commerce reported third quarter final sales rose 0.4 percent versus a 0.3 percent rise in the prior reading.
"I think going forward the important thing about these numbers is that the inventory carried into the fourth quarter is noticeably smaller than expected," Griggs said.

"If you consider that we are going to cut back and try to sell all the inventory in the fourth quarter we should see a much stronger sales and GDP performance, a nice strong rebound in consumption and further reduction in inventories," Griggs said.

"All in all it says we're going to get real growth in the fourth quarter of 2.5 percent or better, final sales of 3.0 percent or better, and a reduction in inventories by about $15.0 to $20.0 billion, leaving no big problems to face us in the first quarter of '97," Griggs noted.
